title: Why is rollback harder in distributed systems than in a monolith — code rollback is easy only when STATE remains compatible; once a deployment writes data in a new schema, publishes events old consumers cannot interpret, or triggers irreversible external side effects, deploying the previous binary may NOT restore the previous system — and why must rollback be considered while DESIGNING the change, not after production begins failing?
shortTitle: Why is rollback harder in distributed systems than in a monolith?

s1_definition.profdef: Rolling back a deployment means redeploying the previous binary, and that is only a true rollback when the system's state remains compatible with that previous binary. In a distributed system a deployment does not only change code; it also mutates persistent state, emits events other services consume, and triggers external side effects. Once the new version has written data in a new schema the old code cannot read, published events old consumers cannot interpret, or performed irreversible external actions like sending money or emails, redeploying the old binary does not restore the previous system — the old code now faces state and messages it was never built to handle. This is why rollback safety must be designed into the change from the start, using backward-compatible, reversible steps, rather than discovered after production is already failing, because at that point the safe path backward may no longer exist.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, "rolling back" is like telling yesterday's clerk to take over again after today's new clerk caused problems. That works only if nothing permanent changed in between. But suppose today's clerk started writing account entries in a brand-new ledger format, sent "payment done" letters to fifteen partner banks, and actually wired real money out of the vault. Now you bring back yesterday's clerk — but he cannot read the new ledger format, the partner banks have already acted on letters he never sent, and the money is gone from the vault. Putting the old clerk back does not undo any of that. The only way to make going back safe is to plan it before the new clerk starts: keep the old ledger format readable, hold the letters until you are sure, and never wire money irreversibly during the risky window.
s1_definition.oneliner: Code rollback is easy; state rollback is not — once new data, events, or external side effects exist, the old binary cannot restore the old system, so reversibility must be designed in before you ship.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Rolling back a deployment means redeploying the previous binary, and that is only a true rollback when the system's state remains compatible with that previous binary. In a distributed system a deployment does not only change code; it also mutates persistent state, emits events other services consume, and triggers external side effects. Once the new version has written data in a new schema the old code cannot read, published events old consumers cannot interpret, or performed irreversible external actions like sending money or emails, redeploying the old binary does not restore the previous system — the old code now faces state and messages it was never built to handle. This is why rollback safety must be designed into the change from the start, using backward-compatible, reversible steps, rather than discovered after production is already failing, because at that point the safe path backward may no longer exist.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, "rolling back" is like telling yesterday's clerk to take over again after today's new clerk caused problems. That works only if nothing permanent changed in between. But suppose today's clerk started writing account entries in a brand-new ledger format, sent "payment done" letters to fifteen partner banks, and actually wired real money out of the vault. Now you bring back yesterday's clerk — but he cannot read the new ledger format, the partner banks have already acted on letters he never sent, and the money is gone from the vault. Putting the old clerk back does not undo any of that. The only way to make going back safe is to plan it before the new clerk starts: keep the old ledger format readable, hold the letters until you are sure, and never wire money irreversibly during the risky window.

**One line to remember:** Code rollback is easy; state rollback is not — once new data, events, or external side effects exist, the old binary cannot restore the old system, so reversibility must be designed in before you ship.

sections.s2_technical:
In a classic monolith with a single code artifact and often a single database under tight control, rollback feels simple: redeploy the previous version and you are back. But even there the hidden assumption is that the state the old code reads is still the state it understands. In a distributed system that assumption breaks in three distinct ways, and each one makes "redeploy the old binary" fail to restore the old behaviour.

The first is schema-incompatible data. The new version writes rows or documents in a new shape — a renamed column, a new required field, a changed encoding. While it runs, it produces data in that shape. If you then roll the code back, the old binary reads data it does not understand: it may crash on a missing column, misinterpret a repurposed field, or silently corrupt further. The code went back; the data did not. The old code is now facing a future it was never written for.

```java
// New version writes balance as integer paise; old version expects decimal rupees.
// After rollback, old code reads balance_minor it never knew about, or a null decimal → breaks.
BigDecimal balance = row.getBigDecimal("balance"); // NULL now — new code stopped writing it
// Old binary now crashes or shows Rs.0 → rollback did NOT restore correct behaviour
```

The second is events old consumers cannot interpret. If the new producer publishes events in a new format, those events are already in the queue or topic. Rolling the producer back does not recall the messages already published, and if a consumer was also rolled back, it now faces new-format events it cannot parse. Worse, in an event-sourced or append-only system, the new events are permanently in the log, so "going back" cannot erase them; the old code must still cope with them forever.

```java
// New events already committed to the topic BEFORE rollback — cannot be unpublished.
producer.send(new TransferCompletedV2(...)); // committed to Kafka
// Roll producer back to V1 → V2 messages still sit in the topic → old consumers choke
```

The third, and most dangerous, is irreversible external side effects. The new version may have already sent real money through a payment rail, dispatched emails or SMS, called a partner API that cannot be un-called, or triggered a settlement at an exchange. Redeploying the old binary cannot un-send money or un-send a notification. The external world has moved on in ways no code rollback can touch.

```java
// Irreversible: the money has left. No binary rollback un-sends it.
externalRail.wire(toBank, amount);   // DONE — the funds are gone
emailService.send(customer, "Your transfer completed"); // DONE — cannot unsend
```

The senior-level consequence is that rollback is a design-time property, not a runtime action you reach for when things go wrong. You must make each change reversible by construction, and the tool for that is expand-and-contract (also called parallel-change): keep the old and new states compatible throughout the change window. For data, that means additive schema changes and dual-writing so the old code can still read, and never destructive changes until you are certain. For events, it means versioned events and dual publication so old consumers keep working, never removing the old version until all consumers migrated. For external side effects, it means gating the irreversible action behind confidence — for example using an outbox so the side effect only fires after the state is committed, feature flags to disable the new irreversible path instantly, and canary releases so the irreversible action is exercised on a tiny fraction first. The key mental shift is that in distributed systems you do not "roll back" so much as "roll forward safely," and the only way that is possible is if you planned the backward path before you shipped, because the window in which rollback is still safe closes the moment the first incompatible write, unrecallable event, or irreversible side effect occurs.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, a new version of the transfer service changes how balances are stored, publishes a new event version, and wires money to partner banks. The team deploys it, discovers a bug, and tries to roll back.

Problem 1 — the new version wrote balances in a new integer-paise field and stopped writing the old decimal field. After rolling the code back, the old binary reads the old decimal field, finds it stale or null, and shows wrong balances. The code rolled back; the data did not.

Problem 2 — the new version published a v2 transfer event already consumed and already sitting in the log. Rolling back the producer does not recall those events.

Problem 3 — the new version already wired real money to a partner bank. No code rollback un-sends it.

The mini-project contrasts a naive change that makes all three irreversible with a designed-for-rollback change that uses dual-write for data, dual-publish for events, and an outbox plus feature flag gating the irreversible wire so it can be disabled instantly and only fires after commit. The demo shows the naive version failing to restore correct state on rollback, and the safe version rolling back cleanly because every step kept old and new compatible.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a transfer of fifty thousand rupees in both a naive version and a rollback-safe version, followed by an attempted rollback after a bug is found.

Step 1 — Naive transfer runs. The naive version subtracts from the paise field and sets the old decimal balance field to null, because it stopped writing it, then unconditionally wires fifty thousand to the partner bank, which is irreversible.

Step 2 — Naive rollback attempted. The old binary is redeployed and reads the old decimal balance field, but it is null because the new version stopped writing it. The old binary cannot show a correct balance, so the rollback fails to restore the previous system. The wired money is also gone forever.

Step 3 — Safe transfer runs. The safe version subtracts from the paise field and also dual-writes the old decimal balance field, keeping it correct and readable. Instead of wiring money immediately, it records the wire intent in an outbox, so nothing irreversible has happened yet.

Step 4 — Safe rollback attempted. A bug is found, so the team disables the feature flag and drains the outbox. Because the flag is off, the outbox holds the irreversible wire instead of firing it, so no money leaves. The old binary is redeployed and reads the old decimal balance field, which is intact, so it shows the correct balance.

Step 5 — Outcome. The naive change was un-rollbackable in all three dimensions; the safe change rolled back cleanly because the data stayed compatible through dual-write, and the irreversible side effect was gated behind an outbox and a flag that could be flipped instantly.

```
2026-10-24 19:16:30 [INFO] === NAIVE change ===
2026-10-24 19:16:30 [WARNING] IRREVERSIBLE: wired Rs.50000 to PartnerBank (cannot be un-sent)
2026-10-24 19:16:30 [INFO] Naive V2 transfer done (now un-rollbackable)
2026-10-24 19:16:30 [INFO] Attempt rollback to old binary...
2026-10-24 19:16:30 [SEVERE] ROLLBACK FAILED: old binary sees NULL balance (state incompatible)
2026-10-24 19:16:30 [INFO] === SAFE change ===
2026-10-24 19:16:30 [INFO] Safe V2 state committed (old field intact, side effect in outbox)
2026-10-24 19:16:30 [WARNING] Bug discovered → disable feature flag, roll back
2026-10-24 19:16:30 [WARNING] Feature flag OFF — holding irreversible wires (safe rollback)
2026-10-24 19:16:30 [INFO] Old binary reads balance after rollback = Rs.950000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Deploy new transfer version, then discover a bug and attempt rollback
    │
    ├─ NAIVE                                 ├─ SAFE (designed for rollback)
    │  balance (old) = NULL (stopped)        │  dual-write: balance + balance_minor
    │  wire money NOW (irreversible)         │  outbox: record wire intent only
    │  publish v2 (unrecallable)             │  dual-publish v1 + v2
    │  ── rollback old binary ──             │  ── disable flag + redeploy old ──
    │  reads NULL balance → BROKEN           │  outbox HOLDS wire (no money sent)
    │  money gone, events stuck              │  old binary reads intact balance
    ▼                                        ▼
  Rollback FAILS to restore system          Rollback CLEAN (state stayed compatible)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Rollback is harder in distributed systems because rolling back is really two separate things that people conflate: rolling back the code, and rolling back the state. Redeploying the previous binary is trivial. But that only restores the previous system if the state the old code reads is still state it understands. In a distributed system a deployment does not just change code — it also mutates persistent data, emits events other services consume, and triggers external side effects. The moment the new version writes data in a shape the old code cannot read, publishes events old consumers cannot interpret, or performs an irreversible external action, redeploying the old binary does not take you back, because the old code now faces a world it was never built for.

There are three concrete ways this bites. First, schema-incompatible data: the new version writes a renamed column or a new encoding, and after rollback the old binary crashes on a missing field or silently misreads a repurposed one — the code went back but the data did not. Second, unrecallable events: the new producer has already committed new-format events to the queue or log, and rolling the producer back does not un-publish them, so old consumers choke on messages they cannot parse, and in an append-only log those events are there forever. Third, and most dangerous, irreversible external side effects: the new version may have already wired real money, sent emails, or called a partner API, and no code rollback can un-send money or un-send a notification.

The consequence I always draw is that rollback is a design-time property, not a runtime action you reach for after production starts failing. By the time it is failing, the safe path backward may no longer exist, because the window in which rollback is safe closes the instant the first incompatible write, unrecallable event, or irreversible side effect occurs. So I design the backward path before I ship, using expand-and-contract: for data, additive schema changes and dual-writing so the old code keeps reading; for events, versioned events and dual publication so old consumers keep working; and for external side effects, an outbox so the action fires only after the state commits, a feature flag so I can disable the irreversible path instantly without a redeploy, and a canary so the irreversible action is exercised on a tiny fraction first.

In my banking work this was exactly the difference between a deploy we could back out of and one we could not. A naive change stopped writing the old balance field, wired money unconditionally, and published a new event version, and when we found a bug we could not restore the previous system in any of those three dimensions. The version designed for rollback dual-wrote the old field so the old binary still read correct balances, held the irreversible wire in an outbox behind a feature flag so disabling the flag instantly stopped money leaving, and dual-published events so old consumers never broke. The principle I take into interviews is that in distributed systems you rarely truly roll back — you roll forward safely — and the only way that is possible is to keep old and new state compatible throughout the change, which is a decision you make while designing, not while firefighting.
